title: Vital Signs
subtitle: Data Visualization II · filter, count & read the plot
story: You're the hospital's instrument technician, clocking off at last — one step from the elevator, and from finally meeting the person you've been hoping to see for a long-overdue dinner up in the break room. Then the pharmacist catches your sleeve. “Before you go — I need a hand.” A shipment of salt-sensitive medicine was being canoed out to a remote clinic when the canoe tipped; the vials went into the lake. The drug degrades in salty, mineral-rich water, but the field kit at the scene can only measure chloride, not sodium. So the question is whether chloride is a trustworthy stand-in for sodium — total salt — across Alaska's lakes. The lake survey is open on the bench laptop.

done.title: Right antibiotic, in time
done.body: Chlorine ran highest in North Killeak Lake, so the infection is Chlorosoma — and Elias gets Chlorocidin. Four reads of one dataset, one life. Your submission code is below.

rooms.designNote: NEW ART. TECHNIQUE — pivot_wider (long→wide) + geom_point + geom_smooth (two continuous), forces multi-variable mapping. STORY: salt-sensitive medicine capsized; the field kit logged only chloride, not sodium — is chloride a trustworthy proxy for sodium (total salt)? TASK: pivot the long data wider (one column per element) with tidyr::pivot_wider, then plot Na vs Cl with geom_point + geom_smooth. VERIFIED ANSWER: yes — a tight positive linear relationship, Pearson r = 0.999 across all 20 lakes (still r = 0.994 without the North_Killeak outlier). ≥6 options describing the relationship (strong positive / a read-off-the-line prediction, vs distractors: none, negative, weak positive). Teaches pivot_wider + scatter + smooth, and SETS UP room 3, which challenges this pooled conclusion. DOORS: first room, single CLOSED forward door = the elevator. TECH: add tidyr to packages (verify WebR build); geom_smooth defaults to loess at n=20, base R, runs in WebR (no mgcv).

question.prompt: Pivot the survey wider (one column per element) and plot sodium (Na) against chloride (Cl) for all 20 lakes, with a smoothing line. What does it tell you — is chloride a trustworthy stand-in for sodium?
options: No relationship — the points scatter with no trend, so chloride tells you nothing about sodium.
A negative relationship — lakes high in chloride run low in sodium, so chloride would mislead you.
A weak positive trend — the points loosely rise but scatter widely, so chloride is only a rough guide.
A strong, tight positive line — sodium rises almost perfectly with chloride (r ≈ 0.999), so chloride is a trustworthy proxy.
A strong line, but only because one extreme lake creates it — drop that lake and the relationship falls apart.
A curved relationship — chloride predicts sodium at low values but flattens out at high ones.

feedback.correct: Correct — logged: sodium tracks chloride almost perfectly (r ≈ 0.999), so chloride is a safe stand-in for total salt.
wrong: Look at the overall shape of the cloud: do the points rise together, fall, or just scatter? Add the smoothing line and see how tightly they hug it.
The points sit almost exactly on one rising line — that's a very strong positive link. Check that it holds across the whole range, not just at one end.
Even setting the single saltiest lake aside, the rest still rise tightly together — so the relationship is real, not an artefact of one outlier.

rooms.designNote: NEW ART. TECHNIQUE — geom_tile HEATMAP (2 discrete × 1 continuous), forces multi-variable mapping. STORY: the lake data is texted to your phone. Which lake is the closest chemical MATCH to North_Killeak_Lake across ALL elements? TASK: geom_tile(aes(x = element, y = lake, fill = mg_per_L)) + a fill colour scale — read which lake's row of tiles looks most like North_Killeak's. VERIFIED ANSWER: White_Fish_Lake (Euclidean distance 257 vs next 363; profile-shape correlation r = 0.993; the only other lake that lights up on Cl and Na — White_Fish Cl 105.3, Na 54.16). Real distractors (next-nearest): Devil_Mountain_Lake, Lake_Matcharak, Lava_Lake, Kurupa_Lake, Kuzitrin_Lake → ≥6 lake options. Threads the salt story (North_Killeak & White_Fish are the two saline lakes; sets up the boss's chloride answer). DOORS: forward CLOSED (elevator → corridor) + back OPEN (→ room1).

entry.title: Going up
entry.text: Chloride tracks sodium almost perfectly, so you tell the pharmacist yes — the field kit's chloride reading is a safe stand-in for total salt, and that the shipment may have been compromised. The elevator doors close. Your phone buzzes: a bush pilot has been pulled from North Killeak Lake and they need you in the lab, and a colleague has texted over the lake survey data. North Killeak is barely studied — start by finding the lake most like it, chemically, so you have something to reason from.

White_Fish_Lake

feedback.correct: Correct — logged: White_Fish_Lake is North Killeak's closest chemical match, so it's the lake to reason from.
wrong: Find North Killeak's row of tiles first, then scan the other rows for the one whose colours match it most closely across every element.
North Killeak stands out because two elements run very high — look for the only other lake whose row lights up in those same two columns, not just one.
Plenty of lakes are 'quiet' (every tile dim) and so resemble each other; the match you want mirrors North Killeak's bright cells too, not only its dark ones.

rooms.title: The corridor
rooms.debrief: The trap, and the lesson. Pooled together, sodium and chloride tracked almost perfectly — until you faceted by park and the single clean line broke into three different ones. Splitting a plot by group can overturn what the whole looked like; always ask whether one trend is really several in disguise.
rooms.technique: pivot_wider + geom_smooth + facet_wrap(~park) — does the correlation differ by park?

rooms.designNote: NEW ART (corridor). TECHNIQUE — pivot_wider + geom_point + geom_smooth + facet_wrap(~ park), forces multi-variable mapping + small multiples. STORY: your crush stops you and gently CHALLENGES room 1 — 'the pharmacist said you decided sodium and chloride track together… but is that really true in every park?' TASK: the same Na vs Cl scatter, now facet_wrap(~ park). VERIFIED ANSWER: NOT uniform — the pooled r = 0.999 is largely manufactured by BELA (r = 1.000, which holds the North_Killeak outlier); GAAR r = 0.675, NOAT r = 0.424. The tight aggregate line hides weak within-park relationships. MCQ: (crisp) 'which park shows the weakest Na–Cl relationship?' → NOAT; or (conceptual / critical-thinking) 'the pooled r was 0.999 — after faceting, what do you conclude?' → it's driven by pooling + BELA's outlier, weak within GAAR & NOAT. Spicier alt pair: Ca~Mg flips NEGATIVE in NOAT (r = -0.43). The crush also plants the weekend dinner-date throughline → the ESCAPE facet-collage meta-puzzle (see escape1). DOORS: forward CLOSED (LAB) + back OPEN (→ room2).

entry.title: The corridor
entry.text: White Fish Lake is North Killeak's chemical twin — nearly identical across every element — so at least you have a comparison to work from. You are three doors from the lab when a classmate you've been hoping to see catches your arm and presses a folded note into your hand: "Some of us are going this weekend — you should come." Then they are gone into the elevator before either of you can say more. No time now — but they had overheard the pharmacist, and they are grinning: "sodium and chloride, always together? You sure that holds everywhere?"

question.prompt: Re-plot sodium vs chloride, but facet by park (BELA, GAAR, NOAT). Pooled together the line looked almost perfect (r ≈ 0.999). Once you split it by park, what's the right conclusion?
options: The link is just as tight inside every park — faceting confirms sodium and chloride always track together.
BELA shows the weakest sodium–chloride link, so the coastal park breaks the pattern.
GAAR shows essentially no relationship, while BELA and NOAT stay tight.
All three parks show a negative sodium–chloride relationship once separated.
NOAT shows the weakest relationship — the tight pooled line is largely driven by pooling and BELA's extreme lake, and it hides weak within-park links.
The parks can't be compared because each holds a different number of lakes.

feedback.correct: Correct — logged: split by park, sodium–chloride is weakest in NOAT and only looks perfect when pooled — BELA's outlier carries the aggregate line.
wrong: Look at each park's panel on its own: in which one do the points scatter most loosely, rather than sitting on a line?
BELA's panel is nearly a perfect line (one very salty lake anchors it). Compare GAAR and NOAT — one of those two is much looser than the other.
The loosest panel has the fewest, most scattered points — the pooled 'perfect' line was an artefact of combining parks, not a within-park truth.

rooms.designNote: NEW ART. THIS IS THE ASSESSED EXERCISE — exercises.csv, '[exercises] data visualization ii' Q1 (dataset alaska_lake_data). STORY (from the exercise): bush pilot Elias Kane was pulled from North Killeak Lake and has a bacterial infection narrowed to five bacteria, each growing in water rich in one element — Sulfuromonas (sulfur, S → Sulfomycin), Nitrobacterium (nitrogen, N → Nitroflavin), Chlorosoma (chlorine, Cl → Chlorocidin), Bromoflux (bromine, Br → Bromostatin), Calcimicrobe (calcium, Ca → Calcihexin). TASK: which element is MOST abundant in North_Killeak_Lake, then pick the matching antibiotic. VERIFIED DATA (North_Killeak_Lake mg_per_L): Cl 337.23 (max) > Na 161.89 > Mg 37.68 > Ca 29.75 > K 8.32 > C 4.3 > Br 1.08 > F 0.11 > S 0.04 > N 0.037 > P 0.001. Among the five candidate elements (S, N, Cl, Br, Ca), Cl is by far the highest → Chlorosoma → CHLOROCIDIN. OPTIONS (the five antibiotics, verbatim from exercises.csv 'answers'): Sulfomycin; Nitroflavin; Chlorocidin; Bromostatin; Calcihexin. CORRECT = Chlorocidin (exercises.csv correct_answer = 3, 1-based → 0-based index 2). NOTE: canonical exercise has exactly 5 options; the skill prefers ≥6 — decide at wiring whether to add a 6th plausible-antibiotic distractor or keep the five as assessed. CODE (exercise): alaska_lake_data %>% ggplot(aes(x = mg_per_L, y = lake)) + geom_point(aes(fill = element), shape = 21) — read North_Killeak_Lake's row. CLUE HOTSPOT: the five bacteria→element→antibiotic table (from the flight-recorder printout). DELIVERABLE figure (submitCodec) deferred repo-wide. DOORS: forward CLOSED (→ the escape phase, TBD) + back OPEN (→ room3/corridor). REFRAME 2026-07-22 (Lucas): the prompt no longer NAMES the lake — it gives the park (Bering Land Bridge) + the flight-log pH (8.04); the student filters to BELA and finds the lake at that pH (North_Killeak — BELA's unique & highest pH, verified single winner) before reading its elements. Adds a derive-the-lake step to escalate the boss. Still MCQ, same options + answer (Chlorocidin, idx 2), decoder key untouched; starter dropped to bare alaska_lake_data (derivation method moved to feedback.wrong[0], per the 2026-07-21 convention); the off-list Na/Mg abundance trap preserved.

entry.title: The lab
entry.text: They are right — pool the parks together and the sodium–chloride line looks perfect, but split it by park and it falls apart; up in Noatak it barely holds at all. Worth remembering. The lab doors part. The pilot, Elias, is stable but fading — a bacterial infection the doctors have narrowed to five suspects, each keyed to a different element. All anyone knows is he went down somewhere over Bering Land Bridge, and the flight recorder logged the crash-site water at pH 8.04. Work out which lake that is, find the element that runs highest there, and you name the bug.

question.prompt: Elias was pulled from a lake in Bering Land Bridge, and the flight-data recorder logged the crash-site water at pH 8.04. His infection is one of five bacteria, each thriving where one element runs high: Sulfuromonas (S→Sulfomycin), Nitrobacterium (N→Nitroflavin), Chlorosoma (Cl→Chlorocidin), Bromoflux (Br→Bromostatin), Calcimicrobe (Ca→Calcihexin). Work out which lake he went down in, find which of those five elements runs highest there — and so which antibiotic he needs.
options: Sulfomycin
Nitroflavin
Chlorocidin
Bromostatin
Calcihexin
Magnistatin

feedback.correct: Correct — logged: chlorine runs highest in North Killeak (Cl ≈ 337 mg/L), so the bug is Chlorosoma and Elias gets Chlorocidin.
wrong: Start from the crash site: filter the survey to the Bering Land Bridge lakes and find the one whose pH reads 8.04 — that's where he went down. Then read that lake's elements.
Only five elements are in play (each keyed to a bug: S, N, Cl, Br, Ca). Among just those five, one runs far higher than the rest in the crash lake.
Sodium and magnesium run high too, but neither is on the five-bug list — restrict yourself to the five candidates and pick the highest of those.

rooms.title: The break room
rooms.debrief: The escape was the whole skill with the labels torn off. Faced with an unlabelled plot, you rebuilt it yourself — pivot the data, plot it, and let geom_text write the names back on — until you could find the point you needed and read the code. That is the real test of reading a chart: you can locate a thing even when nothing on the axes tells you where it is.
rooms.technique: pivot_wider + geom_text label reveal — locate a named lake on an unlabelled plot

entry.title: One more thing
entry.text: The break room at last — and there they are, looking up from a table buried in postcards. “You made it! I'm nearly done — laying out readers' summer postcards for the tourism magazine — but the way out's on a keypad and I've completely blanked on the code. I started the arrangement on the back of the door; help me finish it and dinner's on me.” Postcards everywhere, two editor's notes on the table, and a keypad by the door.

escapeDone.title: Dinner, at last
escapeDone.body: Season down the page, roadside to backcountry across — the three postcards along the middle read 7, 2, 9, and the keypad blinks green. Your crush sweeps the pile into a folder, grabs their coat, and holds the door. The pilot's stable, the infection's named, and the magazine spread can wait till Monday. You made every read of the way — now go enjoy dinner.

debrief.title: How this world worked
debrief.intro: One dataset, read four different ways — pivoted, plotted, heat-mapped, and faceted — until the numbers named an infection and, in time, saved a life. Here is how each room taught a different way of looking, and how the escape was the same skill with every label stripped away.
